title: Bridging gaps in image meme research: A multidisciplinary paradigm

abstract: This work advances the systematic study of image memes as communicative artifacts, developing research methodologies for analyzing their creation, distribution, and impact on public discourse. We provide frameworks for classifying meme content, tracking diffusion patterns, and assessing sensemaking impacts.

methods.name: Toulmin claim-evidence-warrant analysis of individual image memes
methods.description: Applies Toulmin's argument model to illustrative memes about the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio train derailment (e.g., the G.W. Bush/9/11 template and a Bill Murray meme).
methods.evidence: The three major elements of an argument in the Toulmin model are the claim (the proposition the audience is required to accept), evidence (data supporting the proposition), and warrant(s)

methods.name: DRE3 three-tier model: Instrumental, Rhetorical, and Hidden layers
methods.description: Proposes a layered architecture moving from observed meme entities to extracted claims to inferred public narratives.
methods.evidence: The initial Instrumental layer describes empirical observations of the image meme artifacts (i.e., entities such as people, places, events repre- sented in an image meme). The Rhetorical layer identifies the claims that emerge

methods.name: Ecological concepts transposed to memetic claims
methods.description: Uses life history, niche succession, and complex interactions from ecology to frame research questions about how memetic claims emerge, change and interact.
methods.evidence: Some ecosystem concepts that can provide use- ful parallels for queries in a large-scale computational analysis of image memes are Life History, Niche Succes- sion, and Complex Interactions.

methods.name: Fuzzy set formalism for multi-analyst claim annotation
methods.description: Proposes representing entity and claim annotations as fuzzy membership assertions so that disagreement between analysts becomes data rather than noise.
methods.evidence: fuzzy formalisms allow an analyst's process of entity detection and claim identification from an image meme to produce a fuzzy output in the form of an entity assertion or claim assertion

key_findings: The authors argue that image memes function as quasi-arguments whose truncated structure and visual boundary insulate them from counter-arguments.
In their Toulmin analysis, the Bush/9/11 template meme claims the Ohio derailment was a government conspiracy, relying on an audience-supplied 9/11 'inside-job' warrant.
DRE3 is presented as filling a gap by adding an intermediate rhetorical-semantic layer between data collection and inference of hidden public narratives.
Under the fuzzy-set approach, conflicting classifications become measurements of polarization, volatility, or analyst differences rather than intercoder-reliability problems.
The authors state that DRE3 elements can be incorporated piecemeal into existing meme knowledge graphs such as IMKG and MemeX.
key_findings_evidence: the ubiquitous rectangular boundary of the meme—not only demarcates the meme's content but insulates it from the attack of counter-arguments, by cre- ating the illusion of a self-evident non-porous argument.

Since the Ohio train derailment is like the terrorist attack (evidence invoked by the photograph), the derail- ment is a US government conspiracy against its own people (claim), because the 9/11 attacks were a government inside-job (warrant).

The DRE3 model fills in a gap in the current landscape of image meme research, by highlighting an intermediate rhetorical-semantic layer between the instrumental layer of data collection and the inferential layer
conflict in outputs is no longer noise in measure- ment or a problem of intercoder reliability, but, rather, valuable data.
DRE3 could be integrated with existing image meme knowledge graphs such as the previously mentioned Internet Meme Knowledge Graph and MemeX.
